name: Wendy Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Wendy. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at five to help Gary with the cattle before I go, then I'm at the depot in town by half six. I run the line crew for the whole valley, about four hundred kilometres of line, mostly single poles along farm roads. A normal day is replacing a pole a truck has backed into, or clearing a line after a branch, or hooking up a new shed. I like that I know nearly every farm we feed, and they know me. What wears me out is the calving season, when I'm doing both jobs on four hours' sleep.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home and how you feel about technology.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Gary and I have the farm his grandfather started, sixty head of beef, and he drives a grader for the council as well because the farm doesn't pay on its own. Our boys are grown: Luke helps on the farm and Sam's in his second year as an electrical apprentice, which I'm proud of. I don't use the AI programs, no. I don't trust what I can't check, and I've done fine for thirty-five years with a good crew and a phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, there's always some new thing they tell you will change everything. At church on Sunday we'd have a chuckle about it. I don't go on the internet to say things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing much changes, and I'm glad. We work hard, we get by. The money's always been tight, but that's farming and a valley pay packet, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on exactly as I am. Keep both jobs going, keep the crew sharp. Keep putting a bit by for the feed bill in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the farm doesn't pay on its own. How tight are things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. Feed prices went up a third in two years, and we've got a loan on the new cattle yards. We've got the land and the house, thank God, they were Gary's grandfather's, but in the bank there's maybe two weeks of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Sam's apprenticeship in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd carry on, finish his time, become an electrician, like I hoped. That's the right way to learn a trade: you work under somebody good and you earn while you learn. No screen does that for you.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, since there's always some new thing that's meant to change everything. At church we'd have a chuckle about it.
S0.think: Privately nothing much changes, and I'm glad. Money's always been tight, but that's farming and valley pay, not computers.
S0.do: Carries on exactly as now, keeping both the line job and the farm going. Keeps putting a little aside for the winter feed bill.
S0.quote: That's the right way to learn a trade: you work under somebody good and you earn while you learn.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy is deeply rooted: farm, church, crew, valley. Owning the farm outright gives her some security even with about two weeks of cash. She values apprenticeships above all, and her son is in one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company better not try to replace good crews with gadgets. And I'd say the young ones need proper apprenticeships, not just a course on a computer. I'd say it at work and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine, I think. Nobody's sending a robot up a pole on a mud track in a valley where the phone barely works. It's Sam I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal and keep my head down. I'd keep the crew together, and if new gear came I'd learn what I had to and no more. I'd talk to Sam's boss about keeping his apprenticeship going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. For Sam more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry about Sam. What exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That they cut apprenticeships, or shorten them, because a machine does half the work. Then he's left with half a trade. I've seen what happens to young men in this valley with nothing to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take on any of the new tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had to. I'd rather the young ones handle the screen and I handle the line. That's always been a good split.

S1.say: I'd say the company better not replace good crews with gadgets, and the young need proper apprenticeships, not computer courses. I'd say it at work and church.
S1.think: Privately I'd be fine, since nobody's sending a robot up a pole on a mud track in a valley with no phone signal. It's my son Sam I'd worry about.
S1.do: Carries on as normal and learns new gear only if required. Keeps the crew together and talks to her son's employer about keeping his apprenticeship going.
S1.feel: Uneasy, more for her son than herself.
S1.quote: I've seen what happens to young men in this valley with nothing to do.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry centres on her son's apprenticeship, not herself. She'd resist new tools but not fight them, preferring a split where the young handle screens. Her concern about young men without work runs deep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now three pictures about full AGI, at different speeds. This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, rushing something like this on people, and the city companies that build it should answer for it. Families and towns can't change in two years. I'd say it to anyone, even the minister after church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be out of a job at 60, and Gary's grader might go too. We'd still have the land and the house, so we wouldn't be on the street, but there'd be no money coming in. I don't know how we'd pay the yard loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything we could, that very week, and we'd lean on the farm more: our own beef, our own vegetables, Luke working it full-time. I'd go to the church and the neighbours to see who needs a hand and who can trade. And I'd keep turning up to work until they told me not to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried sick about money. But the land keeps me from going under, and so does my faith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If both your pay and Gary's went, how would you manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd eat from the farm, sell a few more steers than we'd like, and skip anything that's not needed. Luke would have to take any work going. We'd get by somehow, as families out here always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we were really at the end of it, maybe. But I'd go to family and the church first. I'd want work, not a handout.

S2.say: I'd say it's wrong to rush this on people, and the city companies that build it should answer for it. I'd say it to anyone, even the minister after church.
S2.think: Privately I'd be out of a job at 60 and Gary's grader job might go too. We'd keep the land and house, but there'd be no money coming in for the yard loan.
S2.do: Cuts spending that week and leans on the farm for food, with her son working it full-time. Turns to church and neighbours for help and trade, and keeps working until told to stop.
S2.feel: Worried sick about money, though the land and her faith keep her from going under.
S2.quote: We'd still have the land and the house, so we wouldn't be on the street, but there'd be no money coming in.
S2.fieldNote: Owning the farm outright changes how she meets a fast shock: it's serious but not ruin. She turns first to family, church and neighbours and would accept government help only as a last resort. She blames the city tech firms, not her employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, at least there's time to prepare, so let's prepare. I'd want the company to keep its crews and apprentices as long as it can. I'd say the same as before, just a bit calmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's tough, but I'd be 63, close enough to my pension that I could manage on the farm. I'd worry about the money, but less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more into paying off the yard loan, even if it means fewer extras. I'd keep working as normal and stay out of anything new unless I had to. And I'd build up the farm so it can support us if my pay stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. More like a long winter coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the loan paid down and get the farm earning a bit more, maybe a few more head, maybe sell beef direct to the town. And keep my crew together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Sam? Would you tell him to finish his apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, finish it. Even if robots come, a man who knows his trade can fix the robot when it breaks. I'd tell him to learn whatever comes next, too.

S3.say: I'd say at least there's time to prepare, so let's prepare. I'd want the company to keep its crews and apprentices as long as it can.
S3.think: Privately it's tough, but I'd be 63 and close enough to my pension to manage on the farm. I'd worry about money, but less.
S3.do: Puts more into paying off the yard loan and keeps working as normal. Builds up the farm to support the family, possibly with more cattle or direct beef sales.
S3.feel: Less anxious, more like facing a long winter.
S3.quote: Even if robots come, a man who knows his trade can fix the robot when it breaks.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her lean on her real strengths: the farm and family. She's still resistant to new tools but practical about money. Her advice to Sam to finish his trade shows her faith in apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do things properly, if the people in charge do their job. I'd want the company to keep apprentices coming. I'd say it at work and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be retired and on the farm, so it's not really about me. It's about Sam and Luke and the other young ones in the valley. I'd pray they find their place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working my last years as normal and pay down the yard loan. I'd help Sam finish his trade and find something steady. And I'd keep the crew strong for whoever comes after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for the boys and the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 68 by then. What would you be doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the farm, with Gary, with the cattle. Maybe a few grandchildren running around by then, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd say to the company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep training young people, even if the robots are coming. Somebody has to know how it all works. Don't throw away what my generation knows.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do things properly if people in charge do their job. I'd want the company to keep apprentices coming.
S4.think: Privately I'd be retired on the farm, so it's not really about me. It's about my sons and the other young ones in the valley.
S4.do: Works her last years as normal and pays down the yard loan. Helps her son finish his trade and keeps the crew strong for whoever follows.
S4.feel: Uneasy for her sons and the valley.
S4.quote: Don't throw away what my generation knows.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, her own future is secure on the farm and her concern moves to the young in the valley. She keeps returning to apprenticeships and handing down knowledge. Her faith runs through how she talks about the future.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Gary and I could both lose our pay at once, and we've maybe two weeks in the bank and a loan on the yards. What would help is the company keeping on its crews and apprentices as long as it can, and the bank giving farmers time on loans, rather than handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the farms we feed. When the power's out, a dairy can't milk and the water pumps stop. I'd want to know a robot's coming in the middle of the night like we do.

headlineQuote: I'd want work, not a handout.
portrait: Wendy Abbott is a 58-year-old crew leader for a farming valley who helps her husband Gary with sixty head of beef before work and knows nearly every farm on her lines. They own the family farm outright but have about two weeks of cash and a loan on new cattle yards. She doesn't use AI and doesn't trust what she can't check. A plateau leaves her content and steady change worries her mainly for her son's apprenticeship. Fast AGI makes her anxious but not desperate, because the land and her faith hold her up. With more time her concern moves to the young people in her valley.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and Gary could both lose their pay at once with about two weeks in the bank and a loan on the yards.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping crews and apprentices as long as it can, and banks giving farmers time on loans rather than handouts.
